answer.felt: That laugh in the pipe going away and not coming back got me — I actually tensed. And then the ledge not being there. That's the good kind of gut-drop, because it's his own fault in the most honest way: he drew the map from memory and the city moved on without him. Nine years of roofs draining down. I love that the cost of his power is that it's exactly as accurate as he is, and he isn't.
answer.expect_next: He gets swept downstream toward the thing that was pushing and dragging in the water, and either gets slammed against it or past it — and the notebook goes under. He comes up somewhere he didn't draw, which means the hollow ends and he's in whatever the real pipe is, with the system counting at him about a circuit he never closed on foot.
hoping_for: The notebook gets soaked or torn and he has to find out what a ruined page does to a place he's standing inside
He works out that ONE CIRCUIT ON FOOT is a usable rule and not just a scolding — that the system is telling him the price, and he starts walking ground on purpose to own it
The thing downstream turns out to be something he can't fight at all yet, and getting away from it costs him something he can't just re-draw

Tull turns out to be why the laughing hasn't stopped
dreading: He surfaces safe in the lot and it was all a scare with no cost — nothing lost, notebook dry
The system explains itself in a long friendly tutorial instead of ruling against him like a clerk
The thing in the water is a generic sewer monster with a stat block rather than something that belongs to the laughing

answer.felt: That first paragraph did something to me — he knows it's the right way because he wrote the gradient himself, and I got the whole rule from that one line without anyone explaining it. Then the pipe being just wet concrete at two in the morning and him laughing, and the laugh not coming back. I was fully in it. And the System correcting itself like a clerk fixing a figure, not cruel, just accurate — that's the scariest kind. The ledge line at the end landed like a punch in the stomach, because the reason it's not there is a good reason, a nine-year city-drainage reason, and he did it to himself with a memory.
answer.expect_next: He gets swept downstream toward whatever's push-dragging in the water, loses the notebook or nearly does, and has to draw something on the fly — probably badly, probably out of nine-year-old memory again — to get himself out. Whatever's coming at him he doesn't fight; he survives by geometry. And the System keeps counting.
hoping_for: That he learns the walked-ground rule the hard way and it stays hard — he has to physically walk anything he wants to draw, so every new place costs him a circuit on foot

That we find out what the laughing in the store was, and it's connected to being counted
dreading: That the thing in the water turns out to be a named monster with a title and a lore blurb, and I'm supposed to react to the name
That the System stops being a clerk and starts having a personality, taunting him
That Tull comes down the hole and rescues him, so the trap he built himself doesn't cost anything
That he gets a power-up out of the drowning that makes the walked-ground rule negotiable
That the nineteen-year-old memory becomes a tidy flashback chapter instead of staying a thing he just knows

answer.felt: That flip — the ledge is under — landed in my stomach. The whole chapter is one idea I actually want: he draws ground and the ground obeys, but he drew it from memory nine years stale, and the city kept building on top of the real one. That's a magic with a physics I can feel, and he's drowning in the gap between his page and the world. The system voice bothered me for a second (clerk erasing a word, rules in caps) but it earned it — GROUND IS WALKED is a hard limit with teeth, not a form to fill in, and it explains why he's in here instead of up there. I read the laugh going off down the pipe and not coming back twice.
answer.expect_next: He loses the notebook or nearly does, goes under, and comes up somewhere the drawn run and the real culvert disagree — a seam where his nine-year-old page butts into concrete that shouldn't exist. The pushing-dragging thing downstream reaches him there, and he survives by drawing something, badly, in wet paper: a ledge, a gradient, a run that ends where it began. And it half-works, because the page is not the ground.

answer.felt: That first paragraph got me — the water going the right way because he'd drawn the gradient, and him laughing out loud in a wet pipe at 2am. I was genuinely happy for him for about ten seconds. Then the chalk line started counting and told him the page isn't the ground, flat, like a clerk, and I understood the rule and the trap at the same time. And the ledge. The ledge killed me. He remembered it right, it was true when he was nineteen, and the city grew nine years on top of it. That's a rule doing the work, not an author being cruel, and I'm sitting here with cold hands.
answer.expect_next: He gets swept downstream toward whatever's push-drag-pushing in the water, loses or nearly loses the notebook, and comes out of it having learned the rule the hard way — that a drawn hollow is only as true as the ground he's actually walked, and that his nine-year-old memory is now the leak in his own map. He survives by drawing something small he walked recently, or by getting to the grate again.

answer.felt: Tense and a little lost in a good way — the fragmented order made me work, but by the end I got it: he mapped a run from memory nine years stale and the city has been quietly rebuilding uphill into it the whole time. That's the kind of cost I actually want. His one hand up holding the notebook out of the black water told me more about him than any stat line. And CLICK 1 / 0 of 4118 hollows is a beautiful ground floor — he has done exactly one thing and there are four thousand more, and the system already told him he doesn't own it.
answer.expect_next: He gets out of the surge or gets carried, and the immediate next beat is June's messages plus that street full of people each with a single white word printing under them — the drain event isn't local, it's citywide, and he's about to learn his walk started it or exposed it. The Bureau shows up on the strength of 'nobody goes below grade,' and Eddie has to decide whether to tell them what he now knows about hollows.
hoping_for: That the count staying at zero for the wall exit sticks — he has to walk it again properly, ending where it began, and it costs him worse the second time
That CARRY, WARD and SOUNDING each turn out to be earned by doing something specific and awful, not handed over
That the notebook is the real power source — his old surveys are outdated maps and being wrong on the page is what makes a hollow
That the other people with a word on the pavement are competition, so Eddie is one of many and not the special one yet
That June is on the surface knowing something he doesn't, and their reunion is a fight
dreading: That the Bureau recruits him and hands him rank, gear and access, so the 0/4118 grind gets skipped by institution
That the thing in the water is a boss he beats now instead of something he survives and has to run from for twenty chapters
That the citywide word-printing turns this into a chosen-one event and Eddie's specific, physical, footsore skill stops mattering
That the status line jumps several numbers at once off-page after a time skip
That the notebook gets destroyed and replaced by a system interface that just knows the map for him

answer.felt: Genuinely good and I don't say that often. The panic is physical — the notebook over the head twice, the ledge that was under, nine years of a city draining into a run he drew at nineteen. That's the thing I read for: he mapped it and the map was old, and the map being old is the whole disaster. And the surfacing beat where every stranger has a word printing under their feet knocked the wind out of me, because up till then I thought this was his private problem. The one thing I stumbled on was Tull and the Bureau arriving as things I'm meant to already weigh — the shouted name landed on nothing.
answer.expect_next: He reads June's messages, and they're her getting a word of her own — she's above grade and it found her anyway. Whatever was moving downstream isn't done with him, and CLICK 1 with 0/4118 surveyed means the city just became a thing that has to be walked, circuit by circuit, ending where it began. He goes back down, and the second run is one he doesn't already know.
hoping_for: That GROUND IS WALKED stays exactly that literal — no shortcuts, no map, no page; he has to physically close a loop, and the cost of closing one is the whole book
That the 4118 hollows are the city's own and other people start claiming them, so this becomes a race over ground rather than a solo grind
That the thing downstream is another surveyor, or something that closes loops the way he does, and its rhythm — push, drag, push — turns out to be its walk
That the nine-years-out-of-date problem recurs: every run he knows from memory is a trap, and the ones he never went in are the safe ones
That June's messages are ordinary and awful — not lore, just someone asking where he is
dreading: Tull and the Bureau getting explained in a lump of backstory, with more names arriving attached to them
That the status line grows a dozen more counters before I know what CARRY or WARD or SOUNDING cost him
The Bureau showing up to recruit him and the story turning into an agency with ranks and briefings instead of a man in a pipe
That the hollow-he-has-drawn line becomes a metaphysics lecture rather than something he works out by walking
June being taken to make the stakes, when her texts are already the stakes

answer.felt: Wired. That last stretch is the best kind of trick — he mapped a ledge that existed nine years ago and the run he drew came out into a city that has been redrawing itself uphill ever since, and the system doesn't care, it just says ZERO because he left through a wall. A survey magic where the page and the ground can disagree, and the page is what kills you. And then that quiet cut to the street full of people all photographing their own word printing itself under their feet — I got cold. The counting isn't his. It's everyone's now.
answer.expect_next: He reads June's messages and they're about the words showing up wherever she is too — she has a word of her own, and the reason she'd been texting all night is she started counting before he did. Meanwhile the thing in the water followed him up, or the run he drew is still open behind him, and he has to close a circuit he can't close because the ground moved. He goes back down to walk it properly, ending where it began, to make GROUND HELD go from 0 to 1.

That the words appearing on everyone is a global tutorial event and the next chapter is a crowd all reading their stat screens

answer.felt: Tense in a good way. The city-flood reveal — nine years of building uphill, and he mapped it as it was when he was nineteen — landed like a stomach drop, because the danger came out of his own nostalgia rather than a monster. And I love that the system is petty and literal about it: he walked a whole run and got a zero because he came out the wrong hole. That's a rule I want to argue with, which means I'm in. The white letters printing under every person in the street, all of them staring down, nobody looking at anybody — that's the image I'll keep. My one snag is the order of things; I got shoved back and forth in time a couple of times and had to re-place myself. But I want the next chapter.
answer.expect_next: He gets the messages from June open and it's bad news about her own word or her whereabouts, then he has to go back down — deliberately, closing the circuit he broke — to earn the CLICK he didn't get, with the thing that pushes and drags still in the pipe. And the 4118 hollows number turns out to be the actual scale of the city's underside, which is what the Bureau's no-below-grade rule is really hiding.
hoping_for: Eddie closes a real circuit and the status line finally moves — GROUND HELD 1, HOLLOWS SURVEYED 1/4118 — and it feels earned rather than granted
June turns out to be alive and gets on the page with him, because right now she's just a stacked phone screen and I want the person
The notebook matters mechanically — that he keeps holding it over his head means the survey he drew is the currency, and out-of-date pages are a real, dangerous liability he has to correct by walking
Somebody else in that street with a word on the concrete becomes a person he works with, so this isn't a solo grind
We find out what the Bureau knows and why below grade is forbidden, and it's something he can use rather than just a boot on his neck

answer.felt: That got me. The whole thing turns on one line — the ledge was under — and I actually re-read it twice before I let it land. He drew a nine-year-old map and the city grew over it, and the system already told him why in the flattest possible voice: the page is not the ground. Nobody explained the rule to him, he just walked into the gap between what he wrote and what's real and it took his legs out. That's the good kind of small. He's got a notebook held over his head and no power at all right now, and I'm more invested than I've been in a first-person-in-a-pipe scene in a long time.
answer.expect_next: He gets swept downstream, toward whatever was doing push-drag in the water, and either loses the notebook or nearly does — and the thing catches up with him while he's still trying to find footing. He survives by using the drawing somehow, badly, and the counting line ratifies it as his first actual circuit-adjacent claim: the water carries him a run and dumps him where he started, and the system quietly grants him the ground he only just paid for.

I've been reading this thing wanting the drawing to be more than paperwork, and it is: the pipe he drew is real concrete, cold in the palm, and it's real enough to drown him in. The System stepping in like a clerk erasing a figure and rewriting it in the same spot got me too — that's the coldest kind of correction, no malice in it at all. And I liked that he laughed. I'm properly in this now.
